title: Half-Life Horizon: First-Order Reactions
welcome_lead: Track the steady halving rhythm of first-order kinetics.
meta_desc: A-Level chemistry adventure on first-order half-life and rate analysis.
final_note: You've timed the universe one half-life at a time.

concepts.def: Time for [A] to fall to half its value.
Graph used to find order and k.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Constant t½ -> first order. t½ proportional to 1/[A0] -> second order. t½ proportional to [A0] -> zero order.

Read three successive half-lives off a concentration-time curve to test.

k = ln 2 / t½ = 0.693 / t½. Units: s^-1.

Alternative: gradient of ln[A] vs t plot is -k, intercept is ln[A0].

A first-order decay with t½ = 100 s has k = 0.693/100 = 6.93e-3 s^-1. After 300 s (3 half-lives), [A] = [A0]/8.

Used in radioactive decay, pharmacokinetics and enzyme-saturated reactions (zero order in substrate).

mcqs.q: Can you determine the order of a reaction with respect to a reactant from the balanced equation?
options: The order of reaction with respect to each reactant equals its coefficient in the balanced equation.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
The order of reaction is always equal to the number of reactants in the equation.
No — orders must be determined experimentally; they often differ from the stoichiometric coefficients.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
The order of reaction is always equal to the number of reactants in the equation.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

mcqs.q: Why does increasing temperature increase the rate of reaction significantly?
options: Higher temperature increases the concentration of the reactants.
Mainly because a much larger fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy; collision frequency increases only slightly.
Particles collide much more frequently at higher temperature, which is the main reason for the rate increase.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
